name: Cattleya
lede: Cattleya is a light reddish purple from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, named for the corsage orchid genus of the same color family.

sections.title: A dictionary name, 1905
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary of color dates the name to 1905, at plate 42, column H, chip 6, hex #A573A0 [1]. No Ridgway or ISCC-NBS plate is recorded for it independently in this library; the ISCC-NBS committee's 1955 match places it among the "moderate purple" names, 6.3 units away [1]. Its Munsell notation is 8.6P 5.4/7.3 [1]. *Cattleya* is also the genus name of the showy corsage orchids, many of which bloom in exactly this range of purple-pink, but the dictionary entry itself does not spell out that link [1].

Its nearest library neighbor is [[eupatorium-purple|Eupatorium Purple]], about 3.9 units away, with [[viola|Dark Lilac]] close behind at 4.0 and [[faded-purple|Faded Purple]] a shade further at 4.9, all cooler and darker [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: A color within ten units of Cattleya covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 12 of 23,781 paintings, as photographed; the wider ten-unit threshold is used here because the usual six-unit match found too few paintings to read [2]. Its earliest appearance is a *Madonna and Child with Saint Catherine* from around 1600 [2]. It also turns up in Eugène Boudin's 1869 *The Mole of Deauville*, John Singer Sargent's 1913 *Sirmione*, and Paul Gauguin's 1892 *Fatata te Miti* [2]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, read as screen colors [2].

origin.named_after: likely the Cattleya orchid genus, though undocumented in the dictionary entry itself
